title: {{NAME}} and the Roar That Shook the Sky
moral: The most heroic thing is not the power you were given, but what you choose to do when someone else needs yours.

pages.content: The Megacliff was three hundred metres of sheer pale rock, and from the top of it you could see the entire Primeval Valley spread below like a living map. {{NAME}} landed on the summit in a controlled burst of gold light, his violet cape settling around him, and surveyed the scene. The valley was in chaos. A vast section of the ancient canyon wall had crumbled and slid, blocking the valley's only river and cutting off the watering grounds where the entire herd of triceratops gathered each evening. Without water, by morning they would be desperate. {{NAME}} could see them already clustered at the new debris field, their horned heads low, their distress a visible and urgent thing. He was strong. He was fast. He could do a great deal. But one superhero, even a very determined one, could not move a rockslide that size before morning. He needed help. He looked down at the valley and began to think differently about who else might be strong enough.

pages.content: He found Bex first. Bex was a T-rex, young and lean, with scales the colour of thunderclouds and eyes like two pieces of lit coal. She was known throughout the valley for her roar, a sound so powerful it had once shaken ripe fruit from the highest trees for a kilometre in every direction. She was pacing the debris field alone, trying and failing to shift boulders the size of small houses with her small front limbs, which was both valiant and ineffective. {{NAME}} landed beside her and she spun, teeth bared. He held up one hand. She held his gaze for a count of three, then lowered her head, just slightly, the way a very proud creature does when it decides to accept help it cannot afford to refuse. {{NAME}}'s eyes were already bright, not with fear or even awe, but with the focused, electric feeling of a plan beginning to assemble itself in his mind. He looked at her, and then at the rockslide, and then back at her. His smile was, perhaps, a little unsettling in its confidence.

pages.content: The plan required precision. A colony of badgers had tunnelled beneath one section of the debris, their work already unknowingly perfect for what {{NAME}} needed: an air gap, a hollow space that, with the right force applied at exactly the right angle, would cause the entire western section of the rockslide to collapse away from the river channel rather than into it. {{NAME}} directed the badgers to widen the gap, three crucial metres to the left. They worked with furious competence, their grey-and-white heads appearing and disappearing from the earth like a complicated magic trick. When it was ready, {{NAME}} flew to the eastern face of the slide and braced both hands against it, pouring every scrap of his strength into holding that section stable. Then he nodded to Bex. She drew herself to her full height. She opened her jaws. She roared. The sound moved through the world like a thunderclap deciding it was something more. The western section dissolved. The river found its channel in a roar of white water and gold afternoon light.

pages.content: The triceratops herd reached the water in minutes, great thundering shapes pressing past each other to drink, their frilled heads dipping and rising. The smallest one, barely as tall as {{NAME}}'s shoulder, drank in the hurried, urgent way of someone who has been frightened for too long. Then it looked up at {{NAME}} with dark, lash-fringed eyes and let out a soft, low sound that was nothing like a roar. It was a murmur. Almost a purr. Bex stood a little apart from the herd, watching, and {{NAME}} walked over to her. She was pretending to be very interested in a large rock. He said nothing. He simply stood beside her, both of them watching the herd settle into the calm, unhurried rhythm of animals who are safe. After a while, Bex made a sound that {{NAME}} had never heard a T-rex make before. Low and soft and brief. Something between a sigh and a hum. The smallest triceratops trotted over and pressed against her great grey flank, as unselfconscious as breathing. Bex stared straight ahead and pretended this was not happening, but her ember eyes were very warm.

pages.content: The valley settled into evening, violet and gold, the river running cleanly between its banks. The badgers had rebuilt their entrance tunnel into something considerably more architectural than before and were extremely proud of it. The triceratops herd bedded down in a wide semicircle near the water, their horns pointing outward like the petals of a flower. Bex had moved to a high ledge above the valley, where she sat surveying everything with the authority of someone who had decided, somewhat recently, to care about it. {{NAME}} found a flat warm boulder and lay on his back, his violet cape spread out around him like a shadow of wings, watching the first stars assemble themselves above. Sleep began to gather at the edges of him, soft and heavy. He was nearly gone when the valley floor trembled once, a brief, deep vibration, and Bex's silhouette on the ledge above lifted her head. In the distance, beyond the canyon walls, something very large was moving. Something that had heard the roar. Something coming to see what had made it.
